problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 2 \\ -5 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +13 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=-2\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+3\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 2 \\ -5 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=5$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}{{5}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$
